headline: What was growing in my night guard case
alt_hooks:
Our school nurse took one look at my night guard case and asked me one question.

"How many sinus infections have you had this year?"

Three. I had never told her that.

Open your night guard case right now and smell it.

I did that last winter. Then I wiped the lid with a white tissue.

It came away gray. And suddenly my third sinus infection made sense.
script:
There was black mold in my night guard case.

Little black dots. Around the hinge. Under the lip of the lid.

I had put that guard in my mouth every night for eleven months.

The week I found it, I was on my third sinus infection of the school year.

I'll tell you what those dots were doing to me. And the promise twenty-six nine-year-olds made me keep in May.

Let me back up.

I'm Renata. I'm forty-four. I teach fourth grade in Fort Collins, Colorado.

I grind my teeth. Hard enough to crack a molar.

So my dentist made me a custom night guard. Four hundred eighty dollars. Insurance paid nothing.

Every morning I rinsed it, snapped it into its little blue case and dropped it in the drawer.

Wet. Closed. Dark.

About sixteen hours a day.

It turned yellow. Then cloudy. Then it started to smell.

I brushed it with toothpaste. It got cloudier.

I soaked it in Efferdent. Eight dollars a box, over and over.

I bought a thirty-dollar buzzing cleaner online. It died in five weeks.

The smell always came back.

Here's what that winter took from me. Remember these.

My voice. Every day after lunch, I read aloud to my class. By January I couldn't finish a page.

My Saturdays. Six miles around Manito Park with two friends. I quit. Too stuffy. Too tired.

And my husband. He moved to the guest room because I sniffed and coughed all night.

Three rounds of antibiotics by February.

A sore throat that never really left.

My doctor called it a bad year.

Then I opened that case under the bathroom light.

I showed it to our school nurse, Della.

"You know the lunchbox that comes back after winter break?" she said.

"Half a yogurt. Zipped shut. Two weeks in a cubby.

That's your case. Every single day."

"And every night you take what grew in there and hold it against your gums for eight hours. Right where you breathe."

Mold and bacteria love warm, wet, closed plastic.

A guard is covered in tiny scratches. The film grows down into them.

Rinsing doesn't reach it. A tablet works on the surface. Brushing just carves more scratches.

Try this tonight.

Open your case. Smell it.

Then wipe the inside of the lid with a white tissue.

Mine came away gray.

That night I made a list on the back of a spelling test.

One. Real ultrasonic power that gets into the scratches.

Two. Medical-grade UV-C light to kill what comes loose.

Three. Tap water only. No more tablets.

Four. Five minutes. One button. I'm out the door at six forty.

Five. A steel basin. Not another dead thirty-dollar buzzer.

One cleaner checked every box.

DentalPULSE.

A ninety-day lab test put seven leading ultrasonic cleaners side by side.

Six of the seven left live bacteria behind.

DentalPULSE was number one.

Forty-two thousand vibrations a second, medical-grade UV-C, plain tap water.

The first night, I dropped in the guard I had brushed that morning.

Five minutes.

The water came out cloudy. Brown flecks floating in it.

I stood there in my pajamas and said, out loud, "Oh, Renata."

Now the guard runs five minutes every morning, dries, and sleeps in a clean case.

No smell. No film on the tissue.

No sinus infection since February.

In March I walked Manito Park again.

My husband came back from the guest room. He says the quiet is suspicious.

And my voice came back.

In February I had stopped two chapters before the end of our class book.

Twenty-six kids made me promise I would finish it, with all the voices.

In May I did. Every voice.

Last night I opened my night guard case.

No dots. No smell.

Just clean, dry plastic.

If your guard lives in a wet, closed case, something is growing in there.

headline: My aligners gave me three cavities
alt_hooks:
Twenty-eight years. Not one cavity.

Then I wore clear aligners for seven months and got three. Right where the plastic sits.

The person who explained it wasn't my dentist. It was the health inspector who once wrote up my kitchen.

Take your aligners out right now and rub the inside with a white paper towel.

Whatever comes off has been sealed against your teeth all day.

I found out the hard way. Eleven hundred dollars in fillings, nine weeks before my wedding.
script:
I paid fifty-four hundred dollars for a straight smile at my own wedding.

Nine weeks before the wedding, my dentist found three cavities. Right underneath the aligners.

I'd never had a cavity in my life.

The aligners didn't just fail to protect my teeth. They were the reason.

And by the end of this, you'll know why I almost didn't smile in a single wedding photo.

Let me back up.

I'm Marcus. I'm twenty-eight. I'm a sous chef at a restaurant in Tucson, Arizona.

Last January I proposed to Alyssa, and that same month I started clear aligners. The plan was perfect teeth by October.

I wore them twenty-two hours a day, like they told me.

But I'm also tasting sauces all shift. Out, taste, back in, all night.

The trays got cloudy fast. Then they started to smell. Alyssa never said it, but she started kissing me on the cheek.

I brushed them with toothpaste. They got more scratched and cloudier.

I bought retainer crystals. About twenty-five dollars a month. Then Polident, because it was cheaper.

I tried hot water to sanitize a tray once. It warped. Three hundred fifty dollars to replace it.

Then a thirty-dollar buzzing cleaner. Dead in six weeks.

Here's what those months took. Remember them.

I stopped smiling with my mouth open. Our engagement photos, every one, lips closed.

I stopped eating family meal with my crew. I hid in the walk-in to pull my trays.

And everything I tasted at work tasted a little like the trays.

Then, in August, the checkup. Three cavities, two white spots starting on my front teeth. Eleven hundred dollars in fillings.

I was still numb at our cake tasting the next day.

The one who explained it was our county health inspector.

Her name is Gloria. She once wrote us up for a scratched cutting board.

She caught me putting my trays in on the line.

She said, "Marcus, you know why I pulled that cutting board? Bacteria live in the knife grooves. You can't wipe them out of there."

"Your trays are the same. Every scratch is a groove. A film grows in it."

"And then you snap that film onto your teeth like a lid. Twenty-two hours a day. That's plastic wrap on a dirty plate, left under the heat lamp."

Whatever sits on the inside of an aligner sits on your enamel almost all day, sealed in, with no spit to wash it off.

Toothpaste carves more grooves. Tablets work on the surface. The film lives down in the scratches.

Try this. Take your trays out right now and hold them to a window.

Then rub the inside with a white paper towel and smell it. That's what's on your teeth.

I wrote my list on a ticket at the pass.

One. Real ultrasonic power to reach the scratches.

Two. Medical-grade UV-C light to kill what comes loose.

Three. Tap water only. No heat, no tablets, nothing that warps a three-hundred-dollar tray.

Four. Five minutes, one button. I have eleven-minute breaks.

Five. Built to last. Steel, not another dead buzzer.

One cleaner checked all five. DentalPULSE.

They ran a ninety-day side-by-side lab test of seven leading ultrasonic cleaners. Six of the seven left live bacteria behind. DentalPULSE was number one. Dentist-recommended. Rated four point eight out of five.

The first cycle, I used trays I'd brushed that morning. Five minutes, tap water. The water came out cloudy and brown.

Now my trays go in every time I eat. Five minutes and back in.

No more smell. Alyssa kisses me on the mouth again. I eat family meal with my crew. My food tastes like food.

At my next checkup, no new cavities. My dentist asked what I changed.

In October I married Alyssa. And in every photo, I'm grinning like an idiot. Teeth and all.

If you wear aligners or a retainer, you're putting a lid on whatever's growing on it.

caption: It was nineteen degrees and I was driving my daughter to school with every window down. The smell was coming from her retainer case. My shop foreman figured out the rest.
headline: The smell in my truck was her retainer
alt_hooks:
Four sore throats since September. Two strep tests. Both negative.

The doctor never asked about her retainer case.

My shop foreman did. In about ten seconds.

My ex-wife and I agree on almost nothing.

Then in February she called me, not to argue, but to ask what I'd bought for our daughter's retainer.

It started with every window in my truck rolled down at nineteen degrees.
script:
It was nineteen degrees.

I was driving my daughter to school with every window in my truck rolled down.

Because of the smell.

It wasn't the dog. It wasn't my gym bag.

It was coming out of her backpack.

It was her retainer case.

And that retainer went in her mouth every night.

By the end of this you'll know why my ex-wife called me in February, and what she asked for.

Let me back up.

I'm Glenn. I'm forty-seven. I fix diesel engines at a truck shop in Boise, Idaho.

I'm divorced. I get my daughter Brynn every other weekend and Wednesdays.

She's fifteen. Volleyball. Thinks I'm embarrassing.

She got her braces off last fall. Forty-eight hundred dollars.

Then clear retainers. Four hundred fifty a set.

Every night, in. Every morning, out, into a little purple case, into the backpack.

Wet. Snapped shut. In a hot locker all day.

It started to stink by spring.

She brushed it with toothpaste. It went cloudy.

Her mom bought retainer crystals. Twenty-something dollars a month.

I bought Polident. Same stuff my grandpa used.

Then a cheap little buzzing cleaner. Dead in a month.

The smell always came back.

Here's what it was costing her. Remember these.

Her throat. Four sore throats since September. Two strep tests. Both negative.

Volleyball. She missed two tournaments.

And her retainer. She quit wearing it at my house because it smelled.

Her mom said it was my house.

Maybe it was.

Then the orthodontist. Her bottom teeth had already started to shift.

Two white spots on her front teeth.

"Is she wearing it? Is she cleaning it?"

I didn't have a good answer.

I sat in the truck for twenty minutes.

The answer came from Luis, my shop foreman.

He's worn a night guard for twenty years.

He laughed. Then he stopped.

"Glenn. Wet case. Lid shut. Backpack. Locker. All day.

That's a sweaty gym bag zipped up in a hot car.

Then she puts it in her mouth for nine hours."

"It sits right on her teeth," he said. "Like a lid. Whatever's growing on it is pressed against her teeth all night. And she breathes over it the whole time."

Then he pointed at the ultrasonic tank in the corner.

"How do we clean injectors?"

We don't scrub them. You can't reach the gunk.

You drop them in the ultrasonic tank and let the sound shake it loose.

"So why," Luis said, "are you scrubbing that kid's retainer with a toothbrush?"

Brushing makes scratches. Tablets work on the surface.

The film lives in the scratches.

Here's the test.

Open the case. Smell it.

Then run a cotton swab around the inside of the retainer.

Ours came out yellow.

I wrote my list on a work order.

One. Real ultrasonic power. Into the scratches.

Two. Medical-grade UV-C light. Kill what comes loose.

Three. Tap water only. Nothing a teenager forgets to buy.

Four. Five minutes. One button.

Five. Steel. Not another dead plastic buzzer.

Only one checked all five.

DentalPULSE.

In a ninety-day side-by-side lab test of seven leading ultrasonic cleaners, six of the seven left live bacteria.

DentalPULSE was number one.

Brynn rolled her eyes when it showed up.

Then she ran the first cycle.

Tap water. Five minutes.

The water came out brown.

"Dad. Gross. That was in my mouth?"

That was in her mouth.

Now it's five minutes every morning, then the clean case.

No smell.

No sore throat since January.

She wears it at my house again. Her teeth stopped moving.

She hasn't missed a tournament since.

And in February, her mom called me.

Not to argue.

"What did you buy for her retainer? I want one for my night guard."

This morning it was twelve degrees.

Windows up. Heater blasting.

Brynn in the passenger seat, singing badly to the radio.

The truck smells like coffee again.

If your kid's retainer case smells, something is growing in there.
